transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Alvarez (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (Valence Head of ML), Amit Rao (Valence Platform), Noah Kim (Valence CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick Optimize demo, walked through prefetched KV cache patterns and batching knobs in the console; ran two back-of-envelope cost scenarios and explained expected hit-rate sensitivity. Agreed on pilot and to exchange security artifacts.

[00:00] Sophie Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — Sophie from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Marcus is our SE, we'll run through Optimize and then dig into some cost sims.
[00:18] Lena Torres: Thanks Sophie, yeah we wanted to focus on concrete savings — our backend is heavy on short chat prompts with long session history, so prefetched KV sounds promising.
[00:31] Marcus Alvarez: Great. Quick agenda: one, show the Optimize console and recommended batch settings for your profile; two, KV/prefix prefetch strategies; three, cost model scenarios; four, next steps for a sandbox run.
[00:48] Noah Kim: Quick ask — we care about p50 latency under 150ms for short-turn user queries, and cost per 1M tokens is a top-level metric for procurement.
[01:05] Sophie Chen: Noted. We'll show how batching and lookahead prefetch can reduce per-token compute while keeping p50 in budget. Also we'll outline when dedicated capacity is advisable.
[01:23] Marcus Alvarez: Opening the Optimize console — sorry if the screen share is a bit laggy. Here is the traffic histogram you uploaded, Amit — looks like 70% of requests are under 40 tokens and 60% of sessions have repeated prefixes. That pattern is ideal for prefix caching + small-batch continuous batching.
[01:52] Amit Rao: That's right, there's a lot of repeated system prompts and small user turns. We currently send full context every call.
[02:05] Marcus Alvarez: OK, first slide: batching knobs. For low-latency chat the console suggests a target batch size of 49to start, with a 30ms coalesce window. That gives decent packing without adding more than ~20ms to tail latency in our sim. If you bump to x8 batches you get better tokens/second but tail latency increases.
[02:38] Lena Torres: Can you quantify "better"? We need numbers to compare with our current per-token spend.
[02:47] Marcus Alvarez: Sure — in the cost model I ran two scenarios against your traffic sample: baseline (no prefetch, batch target=1) and optimized (prefix prefetch + batch target=4, 30ms coalesce). Baseline compute cost per 1M inference tokens: $4,800 (example). Optimized knocks that to about $3,200 — roughly 33% savings, mainly from KV hits avoiding repeated forward passes on the system prompt and from better GPU utilization in batching.
[03:18] Noah Kim: Those numbers look promising but depends on hit-rate. What hit-rate did you assume?
[03:26] Marcus Alvarez: Good question. The model assumed a 58% KV hit-rate on prefixes (based on the uploaded session samples). We also simulated sensitivity: at 40% hit-rate savings drop to ~18%; at 70% hit-rate savings approach ~45%. So it's quite sensitive — that's why sample traffic is important.
[03:50] Amit Rao: How is the KV stored and what's the lookup latency hit? We can't add much on-request overhead.
[03:59] Marcus Alvarez: KV lookups are a sub-ms local memcache in the runtime for the common case (the Optimize sandbox uses an in-RAM LRU + optional external Redis for larger state). In our sim we added ~1.5ms average for a miss vs ~0.6ms for a hit. The miss cost is small compared to a full model forward.
[04:20] Sophie Chen: Also worth noting KV miss doesn't duplicate cost — misses fall back to normal forward passes, we don't double-infer.
[04:29] Lena Torres: Talk us through prefix vs session caching — when should we prefetch?
[04:36] Marcus Alvarez: Prefix cache targets recurring initial tokens — like system prompts or common openings. Session cache is full KV for ongoing session continuations. Prefetch is helpful when session patterns are predictable and you can warm potentially-needed KV entries during idle time or at session creation. For Valence's usage, small prefix prefetch on session start followed by lookahead for next-most-likely tokens gave the best ROI in sims.
[05:02] Noah Kim: Is lookahead configurable? We don't want to prefetch entire long tails.
[05:08] Marcus Alvarez: Yes — Optimize lets you set lookahead depth (1-8 tokens typical), and heuristics to limit by token probability threshold. In the console we set lookahead=3 for the demo. That captured 70% of next-turn hits without exploding cache size.
[05:25] Amit Rao: How do you handle KV expiration / staleness for personal data? Our legal team is strict about retention.
[05:33] Sophie Chen: Good point — we support TTLs per namespace, encryption at rest with KMS integration, and audit logs. For private deployments you can bring your KMS/HSM. We'll share the security diagrams.
[05:47] Lena Torres: On the safety side, if a user edits earlier context, do you invalidate related KV?
[05:53] Marcus Alvarez: We support manual invalidation hooks and event-driven TTL updates. For strict consistency you can disable prefetch for editable contexts, or set short TTLs. Tradeoff is reduced hit-rate.
[06:09] Sophie Chen: Let's switch to the cost model spreadsheet — I uploaded CostModel_Valence_v2.xlsx to the shared folder. Marcus, walk through the tabs.
[06:18] Marcus Alvarez: Tab one shows raw assumptions: model size & perf curve, price per GPU-hour, tokenization, batching efficiency curve. Tab two maps to your traffic: avg prompt len, avg response len, session length distribution. Tab three runs scenarios.
[06:33] Marcus Alvarez: Example: Scenario A (hosted standard): no dedicated pool, request routed to lowest-cost variant; Scenario B (dedicated small pool): reserved capacity with 99th percentile latency SLOs; Scenario C (dedicated + prefetch + higher batch target). Scenario C had the best cost per effective token at scale once commit is justified.
[06:55] Lena Torres: We are leaning toward hosted for beta but may want dedicated for production. What are the inflection points for commit?
[07:03] Marcus Alvarez: Usually when sustained QPS exceeds the free-burst threshold and predictable latency is required. In the sheet there's a commit break-even chart — at roughly 6-8k concurrent short-turns for your model mix dedicated becomes cost-effective. But that number depends on utilization and your tolerance for tail latency.
[07:22] Amit Rao: Do you account for autoscaling and burst pricing? Our traffic spikes are 3x during peak.
[07:29] Marcus Alvarez: Yes, the model simulates autoscaler costs and burst overage. For spikes we recommend a small dedicated baseline plus hosted fallback routing to handle sudden surges — that preserves SLOs but keeps committed capacity lower.
[07:45] Noah Kim: What about quantization/precision impacts on latency and cost?
[07:50] Marcus Alvarez: Optimize flags recommended quantization profiles per model. For some LLMs int8 reduced memory-bound costs by ~20% with negligible quality impact; our cost model includes a quantization column you can toggle.
[08:03] Sophie Chen: Back to the console, I'm going to show the savings simulator — I'll open the "Simulate savings" panel.
[08:11] Marcus Alvarez: Note the slider for KV hit-rate and batch target. You can run Monte Carlo for 1000 simulations; it outputs expected savings and 95% confidence intervals.
[08:25] Lena Torres: Can you share the simulation we ran for Valence? The one with 58% hit-rate?
[08:31] Sophie Chen: Yes uploaded as "Valence-sim-7-2.json" in the shared folder, link in the chat.
[08:39] Amit Rao: (typing) got it. We have a security question — how are logs handled? We need audit logs for each inference and access to KMS rotation info.
[08:50] Marcus Alvarez: We stream audit logs to your SIEM (or S3) and include per-token cost attribution. Key rotations and envelope encryption metadata are recorded. For Private deployments you retain full control.
[09:02] Noah Kim: Okay — assuming we proceed with the pilot, how long to stand up the sandbox?
[09:08] Sophie Chen: We can provision a dedicated sandbox node and console access in under 72 hours once we have the network allowlist and a service account. Marcus will coordinate creds.
[09:18] Marcus Alvarez: I'll follow up after the call with a setup checklist.
[09:22] Marcus Alvarez: Quick technical aside: batching latency vs throughput curve — in our microbenchmarks with your model family, going from batch=1 to batch=4 gave a ~2.6x throughput improvement with median added latency ~18-22ms. Batch=8 gave ~4.3x throughput but median tail rose ~55ms which might push you past the 150ms p50 target.
[09:49] Lena Torres: So where would you set defaults for us?
[09:53] Marcus Alvarez: Start with batch target=4, coalesce window=30ms, lookahead=3, prefix prefetch enabled for known stable system prompts, TTL=6h for prefix namespace. Monitor hit-rate and then iterate.
[10:09] Amit Rao: Are there built-in alerts for hit-rate regressions?
[10:12] Marcus Alvarez: Yes — Optimize has a hit-rate monitor with historical baseline and regression alerts; you can tie alerts to Slack or PagerDuty.
[10:21] Sophie Chen: Let's capture risks: first, if your actual hit-rate is much lower than sample, savings shrink; second, prefetch increases memory footprint and requires eviction policy tuning; third, consistency/invalidations need hooks if you allow live user edits. Anything to add?
[10:42] Noah Kim: Also must verify model outputs under quantized settings for biases — we'll want to run a quality regression suite.
[10:49] Sophie Chen: Absolutely — we recommend running your eval prompts in the sandbox and using our regression alerts.
[10:56] Marcus Alvarez: Quick demo of an Optimize playbook we created: "Valence-prefetch-1" — it contains a runbook with knobs, expected impact, and a checklist for migration.
[11:07] Lena Torres: That looks good. How do we instrument cost attribution per feature? We have multiple product lines and need to allocate costs.
[11:14] Marcus Alvarez: Console supports token-level tagging per API key and per-route; you can export per-feature cost breakdowns and feed into your internal chargeback tool.
[11:24] Amit Rao: Great. Any legal or compliance gotchas for the sandbox? We need an NDA addendum?
[11:30] Sophie Chen: We'll send a minimal addendum and the SOC2 doc. For Private deployments we'll provide a full compliance pack.
[11:36] Noah Kim: Good. One more item — what is rollback behavior if prefetch degrades quality?
[11:41] Marcus Alvarez: We have automatic fallback policies: if quality/regression alert trips, traffic can be routed to a gold (no-prefetch) model variant while you investigate. Rollbacks can be automated or manual.
[11:55] Sophie Chen: OK let's recap next steps — Sophie to send CostModel_Valence_v2.xlsx and the sim export; Marcus to provision sandbox and run throughput sim; Valence to send traffic histogram and allowlist; schedule follow-up benchmark 2026-07-16.
[12:12] Lena Torres: Sounds good. Thanks both.
[12:16] Amit Rao: Thanks, talk soon.
[12:18] Noah Kim: Appreciate the walkthrough.

(Transcript continues in best-effort: the remaining time was Q&A and brief setup details — some short cross-talk and typing noise.)

[45:00] Sophie Chen: I'm posting the shared links in the chat: CostModel_Valence_v2.xlsx; Valence-sim-7-2.json; SecurityOverview_Soc2_link. Marcus will follow up on credentials.
[46:10] Marcus Alvarez: Noted, will provision the sandbox region in us-west-2 and email the service account.
[50:30] Lena Torres: We'll aim to get the traffic histogram and allowlist emailed today.
[52:00] Sophie Chen: Great, thanks everyone.

End of meeting.
